messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 3 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'SECE_Dual': failed the screen and was not tuned (topology 5900617e8561).
L1 L pzp n1 0.001
S1 S n1 out ctrl=G1
G1 SYNC ton=1e-05s phase=0 edges=pos
L2 L pzn n2 0.001
S2 S n2 out ctrl=G2
G2 SYNC ton=1e-05s phase=0 edges=neg
C1 C out 0 4.7e-06
DZ1 D 0 out DZ33
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: -1.8 uW of 0.476 uW needed (-378 %); S4: -1.8 uW of 0.147 uW needed (-1224 %); S6: -1.8 uW of 0.324 uW needed (-556 %)
what this means:
- with the output fixed at 1.8 V, the net power delivered covers only -378 % of the load's need on S2 (heavy load), -1224 % of the load's need on S4 (weakest excitation), -556 % of the load's need on S6 (Cp +20 %, hot) (best of the value presets tried)

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

[c0023] SSHI_FullBridge  (topology 40eae91a637a, score 65.56, conditions passed 4/6)
L1 L pzp n1 0.00081
S1 S n1 pzn ctrl=G1
G1 SYNC ton=1.93e-05s phase=0.0449 edges=both
D1 D pzp out DSCH
D2 D pzn out DSCH
D3 D 0 pzp DSCH
D4 D 0 pzn DSCH
C1 C out 0 1.68e-07
DZ1 D 0 out DZ33
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       1.99       2    15.3   0.144     0.395  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S2       1.96    1.97    16.8    0.15     0.563  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S3       3.35    3.39    84.2  0.0178     0.511  ok       ok       FAIL     ok       ok      
S4       1.23    1.24    11.7       -    0.0693  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5       2.03    2.03    18.9   0.163      0.41  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
S6       2.47    2.48    35.7   0.119     0.609  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      
failing: S4 startup: not reached / not measured (needs <= 0.4 s, margin -1.00)
S3 ripple: 0.08416 V (needs <= 0.05 V, margin -0.68)
S4 vout_min: 1.235 V (needs >= 1.8 V, margin -0.31)
screen (out fixed at 1.8 V): S2: 10.2 uW of 0.476 uW needed (2142 %); S4: 5.64 uW of 0.147 uW needed (3830 %); S6: 6.61 uW of 0.324 uW needed (2040 %)
value sizing: 32/48 evaluations (running)
what this means:
- the output settles below 1.8 V on S4 (weakest excitation) at 1.23 V: the interface does not deliver enough power there
- ripple is too large on S3 (84 mV): the storage cannot buffer the charge pulses against the load

Topologies explored so far (hash: name, best score):
  40eae91a637a: SSHI_FullBridge (65.56)

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo energy harvester.
    *   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a storage capacitor at node `out`.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (Cold start)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (Settled mean)
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and 20M$\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage amplitude: $\sim 0.76\text{V}$ (at S1).
    *   Critical condition: S4 (weakest excitation: $I_p = 8\text{uA}$, $R_L = 22\text{k}\Omega$).

    *   `SSHI_FullBridge` (Topology 40eae91a637a):
        *   Uses a Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) approach combined with a full-bridge rectifier.
        *   S1, S2, S5, S6: Pass.
        *   S3: Ripple too high (84mV vs 50mV).
        *   S4: Fails $v_{min}$ (1.23V vs 1.8V) and $t_{up}$ (not reached).
        *   Screen: Very strong (2000%+ of needed power).
        *   Issue: In S4 (weakest excitation), the power delivered is just not enough to reach 1.8V. In S3, the load is light, but ripple is high (likely $C_1$ too small).

    *   The previous failure `SECE_Dual` failed the screen. It was trying to use inductors to push charge to `out` using switches.
    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` uses a full-bridge for rectification and an L-S circuit for voltage inversion (SSHI). The SSHI part helps flip the voltage across $C_p$, effectively increasing the extracted charge per cycle.
    *   The problem in S4 is the lack of voltage boost/efficiency when excitation is very low.
    *   Wait, $V_{oc} = 0.76\text{V}$ is *less* than the required $1.8\text{V}$. Any passive rectifier (like FBR) will fail because the diode drops ($2 \times 0.25\text{V} = 0.5\text{V}$) leave only $0.26\text{V}$, which is below $1.8\text{V}$.
    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` succeeds in most cases because the inductor flip increases the voltage across $C_p$ before rectification.

    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` is almost there. It failed S4 $v_{min}$ and S3 ripple.
    *   Ripple in S3: $C_1$ was $1.68\text{e-07\text{F}}$ (0.168 $\mu$F). This is quite small. A larger $C_1$ would reduce ripple. However, the tuner already tried values. Let's check the $C$ range: $1\text{e-10}$ to $4.7\text{e-05}$ (47 $\mu$F). $1.68\text{e-07}$ is very small.
    *   S4 $v_{min}$ failure: $1.23\text{V}$ is not $1.8\text{V}$. We need more boost or better efficiency.

    *   *Possibility 1: Better SSHI.* The `SSHI_FullBridge` uses a full bridge and a single inversion switch. A more symmetric SSHI (parallel SSHI) or a more efficient way to transfer charge.
    *   *Possibility 2: Charge Pump.* Maybe a switched-capacitor doubler? But the voltage source is very low.
    *   *Possibility 3: Modified SSHI (S-SSHI).*
    *   *Possibility 4: Inductor-based boost.*

    Let's look at the `SSHI_FullBridge` connectivity again:
    - L1: `pzp` to `n1`
    - S1: `n1` to `pzn` (controller G1)
    - D1-D4: Full bridge (`pzp` $\to$ `out`, `pzn` $\to$ `out`, `0` $\to$ `pzp`, `0` $\to$ `pzn`)
    - C1: `out` to `0`
    - DZ1: Zener clamp on `out`

    Wait, if the inductor is flipped every half cycle (edges="both"), it essentially flips the voltage on $C_p$. The full bridge then rectifies the resulting waveform.

    *Refining the SSHI:*
    In the current `SSHI_FullBridge`, the inductor is in series with a switch that shorts the piezo terminals.
    Actually, let's consider a "Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor" (SSHI) where the inductor is used to invert the voltage on $C_p$ before the charge is extracted.

    Wait, the `SSHI_FullBridge` is a basic SSHI implementation. To get more voltage/efficiency, maybe a "Parallel-SSHI" or a more optimized transfer.
    Wait, look at S4: $I_p = 8\text{uA}$. Power required: $V^2/R_L = 1.8^2 / 22\text{M}\Omega = 0.147\text{uW}$.
    The `SSHI_FullBridge` delivered $0.0693\text{uW}$ on S4. We need about 2x more.

    *How to increase efficiency of SSHI?*
    1.  Ensure the inductor is not saturating (not an issue here in LTspice).
    2.  Optimise the timing ($t_{on}$).
    3.  Reduce losses (diode drops).

    Wait, the diode drops are the biggest killer. A full bridge has 2 diodes in the path.
    $V_{out} = V_{piezo\_peak} - 2 \times V_{diode}$.
    With $V_{oc} = 0.76\text{V}$, $V_{out}$ will be very low unless $V_{piezo\_peak}$ is boosted by the SSHI.

    *Can we use a Synchronous Rectifier?*
    Instead of diodes D1-D4, use switches controlled by SYNC.
    But we only have 2 SYNC controllers and 4 switches total.
    The SSHI inversion already uses 1 SYNC and 1 switch.
    We can use the second SYNC to implement a synchronous rectifier.
    But we need a full bridge (4 switches). We only have 4 switches *total*.
    If we use 1 for inversion, we have 3 left. Not enough for a full bridge.

    *What if we use a half-bridge rectifier (single-ended)?*
    Piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
    If we tie `pzn` to ground, we only have one terminal to rectify.
    But the piezo is a current source. Tying one end to ground is fine.
    Then we can use a synchronous rectifier (1 switch, 1 diode) or just a diode.
    Wait, if we use a half-bridge, we lose half the energy unless we invert the voltage.

    *Alternative: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction).*
    SECE uses an inductor and a switch to extract all the charge from $C_p$ at the peaks.
    Basic SECE:
    1.  Piezo charges $C_p$ to $V_{peak}$.
    2.  Switch closes, $C_p$ discharges through $L$ to the storage capacitor $C_{out}$.
    3.  The $L-C_{out}$ circuit oscillates, transferring charge.

    Let's try a more robust SECE topology.
    SECE Circuit:
    - Piezo (`pzp`, `pzn`)
    - Switch S1: `pzp` to `n1`
    - Inductor L1: `n1` to `out`
    - Storage C1: `out` to `0`
    - Diode D1: `pzn` to `0` (to provide return path)
    - Switch S2: `pzn` to `0`? No.

    Actually, a better SECE:
    - Piezo terminals: `pzp`, `pzn`.
    - `pzn` is tied to ground (`0`).
    - Switch S1: `pzp` to `n1`.
    - Inductor L1: `n1` to `out`.
    - Diode D1: `out` to `n1` (to prevent backflow).
    - Storage C1: `out` to `0`.
    - Control G1: Closes S1 at the piezo voltage peak (edges="pos", phase=0).

    Let's trace:
    1.  Piezo charges $C_p$ to $V_{max}$.
    2.  S1 closes: $C_p$ discharges through L1 into `out`.
    3.  Because $L$ and $C_{out}$ form a resonator, the charge is pushed into `out`.
    4.  S1 opens: $C_p$ charges again (this time to $-V_{max}$).

    But we can use "edges=both" to extract charge at both peaks!
    If we use "edges=both", we need to handle the negative peak.
    For the negative peak, the charge flows from `out` $\to$ L1 $\to$ `pzp`. Wait, that's not right.
    To extract charge at both peaks, we can use a full-bridge SECE or two SECE paths.
    But we are limited to 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.

    Let's try a *Half-Bridge SECE* first (simplest):
    - `pzn` connected to `0`.
    - S1: `pzp` to `n1`, ctrl=G1.
    - L1: `n1` to `out`.
    - D1: `out` to `n1` (wrong way? no, SECE usually doesn't need a diode here if the switch is fast, but it helps).
    - Actually, a standard SECE doesn't use a diode there; it uses the switch. When S1 opens, the $L-C$ circuit continues to push charge into `out`.

    Wait, let's look at the "SECE" topology again.
    The most efficient way to extract charge is to let $C_p$ charge to $V_{peak}$, then flip the voltage using an inductor. This is exactly what SSHI does.
    The `SSHI_FullBridge` was very close. Why did it fail S4?
    $V_{out} = 1.23\text{V}$.
    The full bridge has 2 diode drops. $1.23 + 0.5 = 1.73\text{V}$.
    The $V_{peak}$ of the piezo (after SSHI) was around 1.73V.
    We need $V_{out} = 1.8\text{V}$, so we need $V_{peak} \approx 2.3\text{V}$.

    How to get more $V_{peak}$?
    1.  Increase $L$ or $t_{on}$ to get a better flip? (Tuner should have done this).
    2.  Reduce the number of diodes in the path.

    *Reducing diode drops:*
    Use a synchronous rectifier instead of a full bridge.
    But we have 4 switches total.
    SSHI flip: 1 switch (S1).
    Rectification: We need at least 2 switches for a half-bridge synchronous rectifier (one to connect piezo to `out`, one to connect piezo to `0`).
    Wait, if we tie `pzn` to `0`, we only need:
    - S1: Inversion (`pzp` to `n1`, L1 to `pzn`)
    - S2: Rectification (`pzp` to `out`)
    - S3: Return path (`pzp` to `0`)
    But this is getting complex.

    Let's try a different approach: **The "Parallel SSHI" or a modified SECE**.
    Actually, let's try a **Synchronous Full Bridge**? No, too many switches.

    What if we use a **Charge Pump**?
    A Dickson charge pump requires high $V_{oc}$, which we don't have.

    Wait! The `SSHI_FullBridge` used a full bridge:
    D1: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
    D2: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
    D3: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
    D4: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
    This is 2 diodes in series.
    If we change the full bridge to a **half-bridge** (one terminal of piezo to ground) and use the SSHI to flip the voltage, we only have 1 diode in the path.

    *Half-Bridge SSHI Structure:*
    - `pzn` tied to `0` (via a resistor to avoid floating, or just direct).
    - S1: `pzp` to `n1`, ctrl=G1.
    - L1: `n1` to `0`.
    - G1: `edges="both"`, `phase=0`. This flips the voltage on $C_p$ every half cycle.
    - D1: `pzp` to `out` (DSCH).
    - C1: `out` to `0`.
    - DZ1: `0` to `out` (Zener).

    Let's trace this:
    1.  $C_p$ charges to $+V_{peak}$.
    2.  D1 conducts, $C_p$ charges `out` to $V_{peak} - V_{diode}$.
    3.  S1 closes, L1 flips $V_{peak}$ to $-V_{peak}$.
    4.  $C_p$ charges to $-V_{peak}$ (due to the current source).
    5.  S1 closes, L1 flips $-V_{peak}$ to $+V_{peak}$.
    6.  D1 conducts...

    Wait, if we flip the voltage *every* time it hits a peak, we can keep the voltage at `pzp` positive most of the time.
    Wait, the "edges=both" SSHI flip:
    - At positive peak: flip $+V$ to $-V$.
    - At negative peak: flip $-V$ to $+V$.
    So the piezo voltage $V_{pzp}$ will look like a series of positive pulses.
    This means we only need *one* diode (D1) to rectify it!
    This reduces the diode drop from $2 \times V_{diode}$ to $1 \times V_{diode}$.
    This should increase $V_{out}$ by about 0.25V, which is exactly what we need for S4 ($1.23\text{V} \to 1.48\text{V}$... still not quite 1.8V, but better).

    Wait, if we only have one diode, we might still be short. Let's use a *Synchronous Switch* for the rectifier too!
    - S1: SSHI inversion (`pzp` to `n1`, L1 to `0`), ctrl=G1.
    - S2: Synchronous Rectification (`pzp` to `out`), ctrl=G2.
    - G2: `edges="both"`, `phase=0`.
    Wait, the timing for G2 (rectification) and G1 (inversion) must be different.
    G1 (inversion) should be a very short pulse at the peak.
    G2 (rectification) should be a longer pulse that lasts while $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$.

    But we don't have a "long pulse" controller. We only have `ton` (up to 1ms).
    At 100Hz, the period is 10ms. A 1ms pulse is only 10% of the period.
    So a synchronous rectifier using `SYNC` will only be a "sampling" rectifier, which is very inefficient.
    We need a diode for the rectifier.

    *Let's try the Half-Bridge SSHI with a diode:*
    - `pzn` to `0`.
    - L1: `pzp` to `n1`.
    - S1: `n1` to `0`, ctrl=G1.
    - G1: `edges="both"`, `phase=0`.
    - D1: `pzp` to `out`.
    - C1: `out` to `0`.
    - DZ1: `0` to `out`.

    Wait, can we improve this further?
    Instead of `pzn` to `0`, what if we use a **capacitor** to create a virtual ground?
    No, that's more complex.

    What about a **Voltage Doubler**?
    A piezo is a current source. A current source with a capacitor can be used in a charge pump.
    But the simplest way to boost is the SSHI.
    Let's try the Half-Bridge SSHI and see if it helps.
    Actually, if we use `edges="both"`, the voltage $V_{pzp}$ is flipped at every peak.
    The voltage waveform $V_{pzp}$ becomes a sequence of positive humps.
    If we use a diode D1 (`pzp` to `out`), we extract the charge from every hump.
    This is much better than a full bridge because we only lose *one* diode drop.

    Let's refine the Half-Bridge SSHI:
    - Components:
        - L1: `pzp` to `n1`
        - S1: `n1` to `0`, ctrl=G1
        - G1: `ton`=20us, `phase=0`, `edges="both"`
        - D1: `pzp` to `out`, model=DSCH
        - C1: `out` to `0`, value=1e-6 (start with 1uF to reduce ripple)
        - DZ1: `0` to `out`, model=DZ33
        - R1: `pzn` to `0`, value=100 (just to tie it)

    *Self-Correction on S3 Ripple:*
    In `SSHI_FullBridge`, S3 ripple was 84mV with $C_1 = 0.168\mu\text{F}$.
    Increasing $C_1$ to $1\text{uF}$ or $10\text{uF}$ should easily fix the ripple.

    *Wait, will this Half-Bridge SSHI deliver enough power for S4?*
    - $V_{oc} \approx 0.76\text{V}$
    - SSHI flip increases the effective $V_{peak}$.
    - Full Bridge: $V_{out} \approx V_{peak} - 0.5\text{V}$
    - Half Bridge: $V_{out} \approx V_{peak} - 0.25\text{V}$
